subject: English
name: English, Year 10
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Inclusive and exclusive language
points.brief: Inclusive language, such as we and our, draws people in, while jargon, labels and stereotypes can shut people out or make them seem less.

points.title: Language that empowers or disempowers
points.brief: The way a group is named and described can give it a voice and respect, or take them away, so word choice has real social effects.

points.title: Evaluation reveals values
points.brief: Whenever a writer judges something, openly or through hints, the judgement shows what the writer values.

points.title: Modality
points.brief: Modal words such as must, should, might and certainly show how sure or forceful a writer is, from high to low modality.

points.title: Judging how well a structure works
points.brief: Readers evaluate whether a text's structure and language features actually achieve its purpose, such as whether an argument's order builds to a convincing end.

points.title: Varying paragraph structure
points.brief: Writers vary paragraph length and shape, such as a one-line paragraph for impact, while keeping the links that hold a text together.

points.title: Integrating words and images
points.brief: In reports, websites and picture books, paragraphs and images are placed together so each explains or extends the other.

points.title: Film techniques and representation
points.brief: Lighting, colour, framing and editing shape how a film represents a person or place, such as harsh lighting making a character seem threatening.

points.title: Diegetic and non-diegetic sound
points.brief: Diegetic sound comes from the world of the film, such as dialogue, while non-diegetic sound, such as a soundtrack, is added for the audience and shapes mood.

chapters.title: Language for expressing and developing ideas

points.title: Sentence structures for effect
points.brief: Writers craft sentences for effect, such as a long build-up that saves the main point for the end, or parallel structures that create balance.

points.title: Syntax and style
points.brief: Syntax is the order of words in a sentence, and changing it, such as moving a phrase to the front, shifts emphasis and shapes a writer's style.

points.title: Precise academic vocabulary
points.brief: Academic writing uses exact technical words, such as juxtaposition or characterisation, instead of vague words like thing or good.

points.title: Experimenting with punctuation
points.brief: Authors sometimes leave out or bend punctuation on purpose, such as dropping speech marks, to create a voice, a rhythm or a feeling.

chapters.title: Literature and contexts, and responding to literature

points.title: How context shapes representation
points.brief: Readers evaluate how the time, place and culture a literary text comes from shape the way it represents individuals, groups and places.

points.title: First Nations Australian voices and context
points.brief: Works by First Nations Australian authors are read with their context in mind, including histories, connection to Country and the right to tell their own stories.

points.title: Extending interpretations
points.brief: A text can support more than one interpretation, and a strong reader tests others' readings against the text and builds on them.

points.title: Social, moral and ethical positions
points.brief: Literature takes positions on what is right or fair, and readers evaluate those positions rather than simply accepting them.

points.title: Aesthetic qualities and audience response
points.brief: The beauty or power of a text's language, structure and images, and where it is read or seen, shape how an audience responds.

points.title: Intertextual connections and interpretation
points.brief: Links to other texts, along with structure and devices, open up new readings of a text and change how it is interpreted.

points.title: Evaluating aesthetic qualities
points.brief: To evaluate aesthetic qualities, readers explain which features make a text striking or moving and how well they work together.

points.title: Voice as a literary device
points.brief: Voice is the personality that comes through a text's narration or speaker, and it shapes how readers feel about what they read.

points.title: Voice across poetry, novels and film
points.brief: Voice works differently in each form, such as through rhythm in poetry, narration in a novel and voice-over in film.

points.title: Sustaining a voice
points.brief: In their own literary writing, students keep a consistent voice by choosing words, sentence patterns and details that fit the speaker throughout.

chapters.title: Texts in context and interacting with others

points.title: Representation in non-fiction and media
points.brief: Documentaries, news and opinion pieces represent people and events through selection and framing, which reflects their context and purpose.

points.title: Structure and features of spoken texts
points.brief: Listeners explain why a speech is structured as it is and how features such as anecdotes, pauses and repetition affect the audience.

points.title: Implicit and explicit values
points.brief: Values and attitudes can be stated outright or hidden in word choice, examples and assumptions, and readers learn to spot both.

points.title: Organising ideas for a purpose
points.brief: Authors order and link ideas to achieve a purpose, such as answering objections before they are raised, and readers judge how well it works.

points.title: Interpreting abstract ideas
points.brief: Readers combine strategies, such as questioning, connecting and inferring, to make sense of complex and abstract ideas in a text.

points.title: Writing a thesis statement
points.brief: A thesis statement gives an essay's main argument in one or two clear sentences that answer the question and can be argued with evidence.

points.title: Analytical paragraphs
points.brief: An analytical paragraph makes a point, gives evidence, names the technique and explains its effect, then links back to the thesis.

points.title: Comparative analytical writing
points.brief: A comparative essay discusses two texts together, point by point, showing how each handles the same idea alike or differently.

points.title: Ethos, pathos and logos
points.brief: Persuaders appeal to credibility (ethos), emotion (pathos) and logic (logos), and strong speeches balance all three.

points.title: Rhetorical devices
points.brief: Devices such as anaphora (repeating an opening phrase), the rule of three and antithesis (setting opposites side by side) make speeches persuasive and memorable.

points.title: Spelling patterns from other languages
points.brief: English borrows words from other languages and often keeps their spelling patterns, such as the French endings in ballet and unique.
